title: Railroad history, the 1969 protest, and William Grant Still at Oberlin
summary: Stanford and the railroad, the 1969 centennial protest by the Chinese Historical Society, missing songs for Chinese workers, and learning of Still's Afro-American Symphony at Oberlin in 1975.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: So in 1963 the Chinese Historical Society of America was founded, and my uncle Philip Choy was one of the longtime leaders. He wasn’t a founder, but he was a longtime leader. And in 1969, which was supposed to be the celebration of the centennial anniversary of the completion of the transcontinental railroad, which was held in Utah and was celebrated by the U.S. government, there was a keynote speaker named John Volpe, he was the secretary of transportation. And he kept repeating, “it was American workers that built the railroad.” And he kept repeating “it was American workers that drove through tunnels of granite stone, through snow” and etcetera, etcetera. And the Chinese Historical Society protested, because in fact the Central Pacific Railroad was built mostly by Chinese immigrants who were not U.S. citizens. So this was 1969, May 1969, and at the same time I was ninth grade class president at a predominantly white student school. And I had to leave — to take a leave from school towards the end, before graduation, because my grandfather, who was the last living Chinese immigrant born, was dying. So when I read an article about what happened with the Chinese railroad workers being dismissed I was angry. I never ran for office again. You know prior to that I was often reminded that Stanford built the railroad. Well when I was growing up in 1963 we learned to sing songs in elementary school, songs such as “I’ve Been Working on the Railroad” and “Patty Builds the” — the Irish song. And then there was even the mythical John Henry, the mythical African-American hero was working faster. But there were no songs that valorized, no children’s songs that valorized Chinese immigrant workers who built the first transcontinental railroad. So then when I became a student at the Oberlin Conservatory of Music in Ohio in 1975, I took an African-American music course by professor Wendell Logan, who was department chair of African-American music. And I was introduced to the Afro-American music symphony by William Grant Still, which honored the African-American folk forms and sort of the storytelling of African- American life. It actually had the “I Got Rhythm” riff, which was something that William Grant Still created a melody when he was performing with I think Eubie Blake and the Shuffle-Along Orchestra in 1923. And Gershwin heard William Grant Still improvise it. Because you play the same music all the time. You know, Monk, you commented about how you had to play in a rock group, you know, you’re playing the same music and in a theatrical production you cannot improvise. So to kind of deal with the boredom at times you improvise before the production or the concert started. So then Gershwin, in 1930, he composed “I Got Rhythm” at the same time William Grant Still had the second movement “I Got Rhythm” theme in there. But in those days that was like, you know, the music was in the air.
Yeah. It was like Ellington listening to his guys warm up, and using pieces of their warm- up when writing a tune. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-
